chapter.title: Three checks in five minutes

cards.body:
Stand in the kitchen of the house on photo day. On the table are three pairs of envelopes. First pair: this year's bills, and the cash plus money arriving soon. Second pair: the loan payments due this year, and the cash in the bank right now. Third pair: the whole mortgage, and your own share of the house.

**Three checks are just three comparisons.** For each pair, ask one question: is the paying envelope thicker than the owing one?
cards.simpler: Stand in the kitchen of a house on the day it is photographed. Three pairs of envelopes sit on the table. One pair holds this year's bills and the cash plus money arriving soon. The next holds loan payments due this year and the cash in the bank today. The last holds the whole mortgage and your share of the house. **Three checks are just three comparisons.** For each pair, ask: is the paying envelope fatter than the owing one?

cards.prompt: Your neighbour Dev has 3,000 in the bank, a car he could sell for 8,000, and 5,000 of bills due this year. Can Dev pay this year's bills without selling the car?

options.text: No, 3,000 cash is less than 5,000 due
Only if the bills turn out small

whyNot.a: That's the total of everything he owns, not what he can pay with quickly: the car is not cash until someone buys it.
whyNot.c: The bills are already known, 5,000. The question is whether cash covers them, and 3,000 does not.

cards.reteach: Each check pairs one thing that must be paid with one thing that can pay it. For this year's bills, cash is the quickest payer. If cash is smaller than the bills, Dev must sell something or borrow.

cards.title: Checks 1 and 2: this year's bills
cards.body:
Check 1 compares *current assets*, things that turn into cash within 12 months, with *current liabilities*, bills due within 12 months. Divide the first by the second. **Above 1 means the fast stuff covers the near bills.** Around 1.5 to 2 is comfortable. Below 1 is the first warning sign.

Check 2 is stricter. Take only cash and compare it with *short-term debt*, the loans due within 12 months. Stock might not sell and customers might pay late, but cash is cash. If cash is smaller than short-term debt, the company needs new borrowing or quick sales just to stay current.
cards.simpler: Check 1 divides current assets, what turns into cash within a year, by current liabilities, bills due this year. **Above 1 means the fast stuff covers the near bills.** Around 1.5 to 2 is comfortable. Below 1 is a warning. Check 2 is stricter. Compare only cash with short-term debt, loans due this year. Stock may not sell, customers may pay late, but cash is cash. If cash is smaller, the company needs fresh borrowing or quick sales to cope.

cards.title: The bakery that passed and failed
cards.body: Picture a bakery chain, call it Oven Street. Its balance sheet shows current assets of 600,000 and current liabilities of 400,000. Divide: 1.5, so check 1 passes. Now check 2: cash is 90,000, but a 250,000 bank loan falls due in 8 months. The ovens are paid for and the shops are full, yet the owner spends every Tuesday on the phone to the bank. Check 1 said fine. Check 2 said: not without a new loan.
cards.simpler: Picture a bakery chain called Oven Street. Its balance sheet shows current assets of 600,000 and current liabilities of 400,000. Divide and you get 1.5, so check 1 passes. Now check 2. Cash is 90,000, but a 250,000 bank loan is due in 8 months. The ovens are paid for and the shops are busy, yet the owner spends every Tuesday on the phone to the bank. **Check 1 said fine, but check 2 said not without a new loan.**

cards.prompt: A toy shop shows current assets 300,000, current liabilities 500,000, cash 40,000 and short-term debt 30,000. Which sentence reads the checks right?

options.text: Check 2 passes, so the shop is fine for the year
Check 1 fails: fast assets are 0.6 of near bills, so the year looks tight even though cash covers the loan
Check 1 passes because 300,000 is a big number

whyNot.a: That's check 2 on its own, not the full picture: cash covers the loan, but the other 470,000 of bills still outrun the fast assets.
whyNot.c: That's the size of the pile, not the comparison: 300,000 against 500,000 is 0.6, which sits below 1.

cards.reteach: The checks are divisions, not sizes. Current assets divided by current liabilities says whether the near bills are covered. Cash against short-term debt says whether the loans alone are covered. One can pass while the other fails.

cards.title: Check 3: who really owns the house
cards.body:
Check 3 looks past this year. Compare *total debt*, everything borrowed, soon and later, with *equity*, the owners' share from chapter 5. Divide debt by equity. **Below 1 means the owners hold more of the house than the lenders do.** Above 2 means the lenders hold most of it, and every bad year hurts twice.

The healthy number depends on the trade. A power company with steady bills can live at 2. A small software firm at 2 is worrying. So compare with the same company a year earlier, or a rival in the same trade, before judging.
cards.simpler: Check 3 looks ahead. Total debt is everything borrowed, soon or later. Equity is the owners' share. Divide debt by equity. **Below 1 means the owners hold more of the house than the lenders do.** Above 2, lenders hold most of it and every bad year hurts twice. It depends on the trade. A power company can live at 2. A small software firm at 2 is worrying. So compare with last year or a rival in the same trade.

cards.body: Tomas reads a balance sheet, sees total assets of 40 million, and relaxes. He never divides. The 40 million is mostly a factory, while current liabilities are 9 million against current assets of 5 million. **Spot it when someone quotes one big number and no comparison.** A check always has two sides.
cards.simpler: Tomas reads a balance sheet, sees total assets of 40 million, and relaxes. He never divides anything. Most of that 40 million is a factory, not cash. Meanwhile current liabilities are 9 million and current assets are only 5 million. **Spot it when someone quotes one big number and no comparison.** A check always has two sides, like weighing two envelopes against each other.

cards.prompt: A friend says: 'Debt to equity is 3, current ratio is 0.8, and cash is half the short-term debt. But look at the size of those assets!' Which worry comes first?

options.text: Check 3: debt is 3 times equity, so lenders own most of it
Checks 1 and 2: near bills and loans outrun both fast assets and cash, so this year is the problem
None, the big assets settle it

whyNot.a: That's the long-run check: it matters, but a debt pile does not all fall due this year. The checks that fail on 12-month bills come first.
whyNot.c: That's the one-big-number trap from the mistake card: a number with no comparison is not a check.

cards.reteach: Checks 1 and 2 ask about the next 12 months. Check 3 asks about the long run. When the short ones fail, the company can run out of money before the long run ever arrives, so they come first.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: **Three divisions, five minutes**: fast assets over near bills (want above 1), cash against short-term debt (want cash bigger), total debt over equity (want below 1, judged against the same trade). If the first two pass, the company can pay its bills this year.
cards.simpler: **Three divisions, five minutes.** First, fast assets divided by near bills, and you want above 1. Second, cash set against short-term debt, and you want cash to be bigger. Third, total debt divided by equity, and you want below 1, judged against others in the same trade. If the first two pass, the company can pay its bills this year.

cards.body: Open the latest annual report of any company you buy from. Find total current assets and total current liabilities. Divide on your phone. Write the number down and say aloud: above 1 or below 1.
cards.simpler: Pick any company you buy from and open its latest annual report. Look for two lines: total current assets and total current liabilities. Divide the first by the second on your phone. Write the number down. **Then say it out loud: above 1 or below 1.** That is check 1.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now run three checks on a real balance sheet and say in one sentence whether the company can pay its bills this year.
